## DAILY INTELLIGENCE BRIEFING

### 1. UK deepens Ukraine weapons-production support
The UK announced it will share classified Storm Shadow cruise-missile technology so Ukraine can produce a domestic version. Finland also plans expanded drone cooperation, while Coalition of the Willing members pledged further military and energy assistance.

**Why it matters:** The technology transfer could give Ukraine a more sustainable capacity to strike fortified targets inside Russian-held territory and Russia itself. It also signals greater European willingness to support Ukrainian production as US backing remains uncertain.

### 2. Ukraine faces a major defense-financing and air-defense shortfall
Kyiv says its 2026 defense budget has a €23 billion gap, covering weapons, military salaries and preparations for 2027. The European Commission approved €6.1 billion for air-defense missiles, ammunition and radars, but broader EU funding has faced delays. South Korea reportedly rejected a Ukrainian request for Patriot interceptors.

**Why it matters:** The shortfall could constrain operations and procurement despite new European commitments. Persistent interceptor shortages leave Ukraine vulnerable to Russian ballistic-missile attacks.

### 3. Long-range drone operations are expanding the Russia-Ukraine war
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces claimed strikes on 66 targets, including Russian radar systems, a MiG-29, logistics centers and two vessels associated with Russia’s shadow fleet. These claims were not independently verified. Russia separately authorized temporary state management of critical infrastructure when owners fail to meet security requirements.

**Why it matters:** The reported campaign shows Kyiv increasingly using unmanned systems to attack military, logistics and economic targets deep behind Russian lines. Moscow’s infrastructure decree indicates growing concern about protecting energy, transport, communications and industrial assets.

### 4. Gaza and West Bank tensions remain elevated
Israel struck sites in Gaza it described as Hamas infrastructure and weapons storage; Palestinian reports said a mosque and desalination facility were also hit. Israel warned of expanded action if kite, balloon and drone launches continue. In the West Bank, settler attacks and Israeli raids have intensified while the E1 settlement project advances.

**Why it matters:** Even limited incidents could undermine the Gaza ceasefire and delay reconstruction and disarmament arrangements. The E1 project and escalating settler violence further weaken prospects for a contiguous Palestinian state.

### 5. Iran signals resistance to US pressure
Iran said it would not accept an end to the conflict on terms set by what it called the “aggressive” parties and warned countries against allowing their territory or facilities to support attacks. Tehran also condemned the new US sanctions campaign and disputed Washington’s characterization of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

**Why it matters:** The statements indicate that the ceasefire remains politically fragile. Renewed confrontation could again threaten US regional bases and shipping through a critical energy corridor.

## WATCH

- **Red Sea escalation:** Yemen’s Houthis claimed a ballistic-missile strike on a Saudi oil tanker and attacks on Saudi forces. The claims require independent confirmation, but any verified attack could widen regional hostilities.
- **Sudan-Chad spillover:** Chad accused aircraft or drones linked to Sudan’s war of conducting strikes more than 100km inside Chadian territory and placed its forces on high alert.
- **South Sudan instability:** Two UN peacekeepers were killed in an ambush in Jonglei amid the collapse of the 2018 peace framework and growing concern about renewed civil war.

## 1. Chinese official-vessel activity around Taiwan reaches new high

**What happened:** Taiwan’s defence ministry recorded 118 detections of Chinese coastguard, survey and other official vessels during the first 24 days of August—surpassing the monthly records set in June and July. Activity was concentrated east of Taiwan, including waters where Chinese, Japanese and Philippine maritime claims overlap.

**Why it matters:** The sustained presence signals increased Chinese maritime pressure around Taiwan and in disputed regional waters. It raises the risk of confrontations involving Taiwan, Japan, the Philippines or commercial shipping, particularly following planned Japan-Philippines maritime boundary talks.

## 2. South Korea rejects Ukrainian request for Patriot interceptors

**What happened:** According to the *Chosun Ilbo*, Ukraine requested PAC-3 interceptor missiles during a July visit by a senior Ukrainian adviser. Seoul rejected the request on August 10, citing Korean Peninsula contingencies and reaffirming its policy against supplying lethal weapons to Ukraine. Alternatives involving South Korea’s Cheongung-II system were reportedly constrained by existing export commitments.

**Why it matters:** The decision underscores Seoul’s priority of preserving air-defence stocks amid the North Korean threat. It also limits potential Asian support for Ukraine’s depleted air-defence capabilities and shows that South Korea remains unwilling to shift from financial and non-lethal assistance to direct arms transfers.

## 3. Fresh violence erupts in India’s Manipur state

**What happened:** Several houses were burned and gunfire broke out between two groups in Manipur, injuring a security officer. The incident follows three years of ethnic and religiously charged violence in the northeastern state.

**Why it matters:** Renewed clashes indicate that the conflict remains unresolved and could again threaten civilian security, displacement conditions and political stability. Continued violence may also place additional pressure on India’s central and state authorities to restore order and pursue a durable settlement.

## WATCH

- **Taiwan-area maritime operations:** Monitor whether China sustains or further expands coastguard and survey activity, and whether encounters with Japanese, Philippine or Taiwanese forces become more confrontational.
- **China’s lunar programme:** The Chang’e 7 south-pole mission has reportedly been delayed until at least 2027, potentially affecting China’s timetable for water exploration and its planned crewed and joint lunar-base programmes.

### UK transfers Storm Shadow production technology to Ukraine

The UK agreed to share classified technical information enabling Ukraine to produce a domestic version of the Storm Shadow long-range cruise missile. France has reportedly taken a similar step. The decision was announced during a UK leadership visit to Kyiv and a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing.

**Why it matters:** Domestic production could increase Ukraine’s supply of precision missiles and reduce dependence on foreign deliveries and political approvals. Sharing sensitive weapons technology also sets a significant precedent for European defense cooperation with Ukraine.

### Ukraine faces €23 billion defense-budget shortfall

Kyiv said it needs approximately €23 billion to cover military salaries, compensation for fallen soldiers’ families, weapons procurement and preparations for early 2027. The European Commission approved €6.1 billion for air-defense missiles, ammunition and radars, but this covers only part of the gap. Delays affecting a broader EU loan package have increased pressure on Ukraine’s finances.

**Why it matters:** A prolonged funding shortage could disrupt procurement and personnel payments at a critical stage of the war. It also highlights Ukraine’s continuing dependence on timely European financing as US support remains uncertain.

### Drone campaign expands as Russia tightens infrastructure controls

Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces claimed strikes against 66 targets in one night, including Russian aircraft, radars, military positions, logistics facilities and vessels linked to the shadow fleet. Some claims have not been independently verified. Separately, President Vladimir Putin authorized temporary state management of Russian critical infrastructure when owners fail to implement security or repair measures.

**Why it matters:** The developments indicate an expanding campaign against targets deep inside Russia and occupied territory, including military, logistics and economic assets. Moscow’s decree suggests heightened concern about the vulnerability of energy, transport, communications and industrial infrastructure.

### WATCH

- **European aid delivery:** Whether partners close Ukraine’s remaining defense-budget gap and convert Coalition of the Willing pledges into timely funding, air defense and ammunition.
- **Escalation and diplomacy:** Further Ukrainian deep strikes and Russian retaliation could complicate already-stalled Russian-US contacts and broader ceasefire efforts.

### Iran rejects pressure over ceasefire and sanctions

Iran said it would not accept war-ending terms imposed by the United States or Israel and denounced Washington’s new sanctions campaign and naval blockade as aggression. Tehran also disputed US claims that the Strait of Hormuz was operating normally and warned that countries allowing their territory or bases to support attacks could face retaliation.

**Why it matters:** The statements indicate continued risk to the Iran ceasefire, regional US facilities and energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Further sanctions or military action could trigger renewed conflict and wider economic disruption.

### Houthis strike Saudi-linked tanker in Red Sea

Saudi shipping company Bahri confirmed that the *Amzan* was hit in the Red Sea west of Yanbu after Yemen’s Houthis claimed a ballistic-missile attack. The crew was safe, with no injuries or reported environmental damage. The Houthis also claimed attacks on Saudi forces and convoys in Yemen.

**Why it matters:** The strike threatens Saudi Arabia’s principal Red Sea oil-export route, which has become more important because of disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. Continued attacks could raise shipping costs, constrain oil exports and renew direct Saudi-Houthi escalation.

### Israel conducts Gaza strikes amid renewed kite launches

Israel struck what it described as Hamas infrastructure and weapons-storage facilities in Gaza City’s Shati area after several kites carrying Arabic messages landed in Israeli border communities. The kites reportedly contained no incendiary material or explosives. Palestinian reports said a mosque and desalination facility were struck; no immediate casualties were reported. Separately, Israel said it killed an alleged Hamas Nukhba member in Deir al-Balah who was planning attacks and rebuilding capabilities.

**Why it matters:** The operations show how limited incidents can generate renewed military action despite the reported ceasefire. Israeli threats to expand strikes and evacuate areas used for launches could further delay reconstruction and increase risks to civilians and aid infrastructure.

### WATCH

- **West Bank:** Monitor the E1 settlement plan, rising settler attacks and Israeli security raids, which could intensify unrest and further complicate prospects for a contiguous Palestinian state.
- **Syria:** Persistent bombings, assassinations and ambushes—many reportedly linked to Islamic State cells—are testing the post-Assad government’s security capacity.

### US–Canada trade conflict escalates

US President Donald Trump said tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel would rise to 50% from January 2027 after bilateral trade talks collapsed. Separate 50% duties on about $20 billion of Canadian goods have already taken effect, prompting Prime Minister Mark Carney to announce dollar-for-dollar retaliation beginning on 8 September. Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Canada should be prepared to restrict electricity and critical-mineral exports if the dispute worsens.

**Why it matters:** The measures threaten highly integrated North American automotive, steel and energy supply chains. Any Canadian restrictions on nickel, uranium, electricity, oil or potash could affect US manufacturing, energy security and defence-related supply chains.

### Haitian gangs expand attacks beyond the capital

The Viv Ansanm gang coalition attacked Kenscoff, a farming community above Port-au-Prince, killing multiple residents and burning homes. The final death toll remains unclear because of access and communication problems. Gangs already control an estimated 70% of the capital, while violence has displaced about 1.5 million people nationwide.

**Why it matters:** The attack demonstrates gangs’ ability to project violence into previously safer communities and further erodes state control. Continued insecurity threatens humanitarian access and preparations for Haiti’s planned December elections, the first general elections in more than a decade.

### Cartel allegations deepen political tensions in Mexico

Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha briefly returned to office before reversing course after President Claudia Sheinbaum said the move was inappropriate. US prosecutors charged Rocha in April with conspiring with the Sinaloa Cartel in exchange for bribes and political support; he denies the allegations. Sinaloa’s legislature is expected to appoint an interim governor.

**Why it matters:** The case places pressure on Mexico’s ruling Morena party and could complicate US–Mexico security cooperation over drug trafficking. It also raises governance concerns in a state central to cartel activity.

### WATCH

- **US–Canada retaliation:** Whether Ottawa or Ontario moves beyond tariffs to restrict electricity, critical minerals or other strategic commodities.
- **Haiti’s election timetable:** Whether worsening gang violence forces changes to the planned December vote or prompts a stronger international security response.

articles.title: UK to help Ukraine build Storm Shadow long-range missiles: Why it matters
articles.body:
UK to help Ukraine build Storm Shadow long-range missiles: Why it matters
The UK’s willingness to share classified missile-production knowledge sets a potentially important precedent.
The United Kingdom is set to share classified weapons information with Ukraine to enable it to produce its own version of the Storm Shadow long-range cruise missile, designed jointly with France, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham visits Kyiv on his first foreign trip as the UK’s prime minister.
Burnham’s trip on Monday, timed to coincide with Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence from the Soviet Union, is the latest show of support on the part of the UK and Ukraine’s other European allies at a time when backing from the United States has been erratic, analysts said.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Russia, Ukraine trade attacks as Putin warns of ‘far more destructive’ hits
- list 2 of 3Putin warns Ukraine has opened ‘Pandora’s box’, rejects peace proposals
- list 3 of 3Zelenskyy says wartime elections could ‘destroy’ Ukraine
Burnham described Russia’s war on Ukraine as “four and a half years of Russia’s full-scale invasion … aimed at crushing the independence we are here to celebrate” as he appeared alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a ceremony in Kyiv.
“But today and every day, you prove that they have failed.”
Burnham is also to co-chair a meeting of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, those nations prepared to provide support for war-torn Ukraine.
The sharing of top-secret weapons blueprints stands in contrast to US President Donald Trump’s backpedalling last month on a promise to allow Ukraine to manufacture its own version of the US-made Patriot air defence interceptor, which Ukraine says it badly needs to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.
While the US has provided Ukraine with US-made Patriot air defence batteries and munitions in the past, Trump last month said handing over the underlying technology to Ukraine to be able to independently produce them was “a hard thing to give away”.
The UK’s decision to share blueprints, however, follows a similar move by France and comes as Ukraine and Russia exchange heavy air attacks and Russian President Vladimir Putin warns of intensified retaliatory strikes on Ukrainian economic infrastructure.
Ukraine has stepped up its domestic military production, crafting long-range drones and missiles that strike deep into Russian territory, but analysts said producing its own Storm Shadows will give Kyiv the ability to hit Russia’s strategic targets more efficiently and at an unprecedented rate.
What are Storm Shadow long-range missiles?
Also known as SCALP in France, these missiles have a range of about 560km (350 miles) and are capable of hitting targets 240km (150 miles) inside Russian territory. This is not as far as Ukraine’s in-house, deep-strike drones, such as the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile, which has a range of 3,000km (1,865 miles).
But while Ukrainian long-range missiles can hit “soft” targets inside Russia, such as Wildberries warehouses, Storm Shadow missiles give Kyiv the ability to hit “hard” targets, including heavily fortified, guarded locations that are usually protected by much tougher defences.
Their advanced navigation systems also mean they can be used at night and in all weather conditions.
Last year, the Ukrainian military’s General Staff said Storm Shadow missiles made by the manufacturer MBDA and provided by the UK had been used to hit Russian facilities, including a chemical plant and the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery, one of the biggest oil product suppliers in southern Russia. This year, they were used to attack Russia’s Black Sea naval headquarters in the port city of Sevastopol in Crimea.
One Storm Shadow missile is estimated to cost about $1m to produce, so they are deployed in more carefully calibrated attacks than the flurry of cheap drones that Ukraine already mass-produces.
How easy will it be for Ukraine to build its own Storm Shadow missiles?
Keir Giles, an associate fellow at the Chatham House think tank, said Ukraine is likely to have a good capacity for producing these more sophisticated weapon systems once it has the blueprints.
“Ukraine, under the force of fighting a war of national survival, has been developing a very agile, highly motivated and distributed defence industry, which is far ahead in terms of adaptation to current needs [compared with] some of its Western European counterparts, including the UK,” he told Al Jazeera.
Being able to produce higher quantities of this missile, more than its actual capability, is what could make the difference, he added.
“Ukraine has had to be highly selective in the targets against which it uses its very limited stocks of the most advanced weapons systems,” Giles said. “Russia, meanwhile, has been exponentially increasing its production of drones and missiles, a trend that’s been in place for several years now.”
“So redressing that balance would be a major step forward for Ukraine, especially if it is able to reduce the number of missiles being launched at Ukraine every night by striking at the facilities that enable those launches,” the analyst added.
Has Ukraine been able to produce any of its own long-range missiles?
Yes. Besides its mass production of cheap short-range drones and interceptors, Ukraine is capable of designing and manufacturing more sophisticated longer-range missile systems, including the Neptune and Flamingo cruise missiles.
Karan Vassil, a Eurasia analyst at the UK-based private intelligence firm Sibylline, said Ukraine has also been developing and testing its own ballistic missile systems.
However, the Storm Shadow/SCALP “is a highly sophisticated weapons system incorporating decades of Anglo-French research and development”, Vassil told Al Jazeera. “Licensed production gives Ukraine access to knowledge and industrial processes that would otherwise take considerable time and resources to reproduce.”
Giles, who also leads the Conflict Studies Research Centre, a group of experts in Eurasian security, said Ukraine may well already have knowledge of the design of Storm Shadow missiles but using it without cooperation would be a “slap in the face to its coalition supporters”.
The reason Ukraine is only now getting access to the missiles’ blueprints has to do with politics, he said. “The United States is not willing to supply the interceptors for Patriot missile systems, so there’s a gap in Ukraine’s air and missile defences, which Russia has been exploiting.”
He added: “European partners are taking up the task of making sure that Ukraine can prevail in the war, and a major part of that is ensuring that it can strike into Russia.”
Vassil said British and French willingness to transfer classified missile-production knowledge sets a potentially important precedent for future allied cooperation. “But it remains uncertain whether this will have an impact on Washington’s posture regarding Patriot interceptors,” he said.
How fast can Ukraine scale up production of Storm Shadow missiles?
France and the UK have expressed hope that they can help Ukraine set up a production line by the end of the year.
However, estimates suggested a new batch of cruise missiles of this complexity could take about two years from contract award to delivery, according to Vassil, who added that establishing production will be a challenging endeavour and will most likely continue to depend on a complex international supply chain.
Storm Shadows also incorporate some sensitive US technologies, meaning some aspects of supply or transfer may still require US approval and “it remains uncertain how this will apply to Ukrainian production”, he said.
There are also substantial security challenges. “Missile-production facilities inside Ukraine would present valuable targets for Russia and would have to operate under the continuing threat of Russian long-range missile and drone attacks,” Vassil continued.
“Protecting production sites, dispersing manufacturing and maintaining supplies of critical components could, therefore, become almost as important as obtaining the technical information itself.”

articles.title: Ukraine faces €23B defense funding hole as Western cash comes too slow
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomes international leaders upon their arrival for the Coalition of the Willing meeting, in Kyiv on Aug. 24, 2026. | Pool photo by Henry Nicholls via AFP/Getty Images
KYIV — Ukraine faces a €23 billion hole in its defense budget this year, leaving Kyiv scrambling for cash to fight Russia even as Western leaders gathered in the capital to mark the country's independence day and pledge ongoing support.
The money is needed not only for weapons and air defense, but also to pay soldiers, support the families of those killed and ensure Ukraine has the supplies it needs to start 2027.
“We are not asking [you] to fight for us. Give Ukraine everything to stop this war, to stop it faster than Putin can start the next one,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a speech Monday.
Advertisement
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham was in Kyiv Monday for a meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing.
European Council President António Costa, Luxembourgish Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Moldovan President Maia Sandu, Estonian President Alar Karis, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and other Nordic and Baltic leaders also attended in person, while French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz joined remotely.
“Ukrainian people deserve not just continued support but our gratitude ... I am determined we [the coalition of the willing] will work together to deliver the support you need,” Burnham said in a statement.
The funding gap originated after the defense ministry brought forward spending originally planned for the second half of the year, while the EU’s €90 billion loan was delayed by roadblocks from Hungary.
“At the beginning of the year, decisions were made at the ministry to use in the first half of the year funds that were intended to be disbursed in the second half," Zelenskyy said during a meeting with reporters on Saturday. The shortfall comes on top of €30 billion in funding Europe has already pledged to Ukraine this year as part of the €90 billion loan.
Purchases made included "fiber-optic drones, middle-strike drones, interceptors,” former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov told POLITICO in June.
Advertisement
"Now, in the second half of the year, those funds need to be compensated for and supplemented,” Zelenskyy added.
The European Commission offered some relief Monday, approving €6.1 billion in new defense procurement for Ukraine. This latest disbursement from the EU’s €90 billion loan package will fund air-defense missiles and ammunition, as well as radars — among Kyiv’s most urgent needs. But the money falls far short of what Ukraine says it requires.
Ukraine needs about €6.8 billion to €8.5 billion to ensure a “normal start” to next year, the Ukrainian leader said. That money is effectively needed in advance to pay for weapons and other supplies for January 2027. Around €17 billion more is needed for military salaries, payments to the families of fallen soldiers and other expenses.
“A lot of money is needed,” he added.
But domestic politics are also creating obstacles to international funding. Zelenskyy admitted that Ukrainian lawmakers are stalling the implementation of reforms on which some international aid is conditional.
Overall, parliament is currently delaying 24 reform bills tied to Western funding disbursement. While not all the funds are tied to defense spending, getting EU money would free up Ukraine's scarce resources for other urgent defense needs.
Advertisement
Last week, the Ukrainian parliament’s law enforcement committee removed five government and judicial reform bills from consideration because they are no longer relevant, Ukrainian MP Anastasiya Radina said last week.
Maksym Buzhanskiy, a lawmaker from Zelenskyy's party, defended the committee's decision to remove the bills, claiming they do not correspond to Ukraine commitments needed for EU funding.
Zelenskyy is planning to ask for disbursement of EU funds ahead of schedule.
“I am working on this with the French and the Germans. Practically, we need to bring forward the second portion of the European funds allocated for Ukraine, and this is an extremely difficult task,” Zelenskyy said.

articles.title: Ukraine’s robot and drone parade offers a glimpse of the future of war
articles.body:
Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day with a military display unlike any it had staged before: robots on the streets of Kyiv, naval drones on the Dnipro river and UAVs in the skies above the capital, showcasing technologies that have transformed the battlefield since Russia’s full-scale invasion.
There were no marching soldiers, no tanks and no columns of heavy armour. In their place came robots designed to perform many of the same tasks.
Marking 35 years of independence, Ukraine staged a different kind of military parade on Monday, showcasing its defence technology and unmanned warfare capabilities.
The parade offered a glimpse of the future of warfare and how profoundly four and a half years of Russia’s full-scale invasion have transformed the Ukrainian military.
Dozens of multi-role unmanned ground vehicles moved along Khreshchatyk, Kyiv’s main street, including robotic systems designed for combat, reconnaissance, logistics and the evacuation of wounded soldiers from the battlefield.
On the Dnipro river, Ukraine displayed the naval drones that have helped it challenge Russia’s once-dominant Black Sea Fleet despite possessing no conventional fleet of comparable size.
They included variants of the Magura and Sea Baby families of unmanned vessels, which Ukraine has used to strike Russian warships, military infrastructure and other targets.
Above the capital flew another generation of machines that has become indispensable on Ukraine’s battlefields: reconnaissance and strike UAVs, alongside interceptor drones developed to shoot down Russian drones attacking Ukrainian cities around the clock.
The parade offered a snapshot of a military transformation that has taken place at extraordinary speed and scale since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Four and a half years later unmanned systems have become central to operations across land, sea and air, performing tasks once entrusted overwhelmingly to soldiers, aircraft, ships and armoured vehicles.
In 2024, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed legislation creating the Unmanned Systems Forces — a separate branch of the military dedicated to drone warfare — making Ukraine the first country to establish an independent branch built around unmanned systems.
The innovation reflects both technological development and brutal necessity.
Ukraine is defending itself against a much larger country with greater reserves of soldiers and conventional weapons.
Unmanned systems have allowed Kyiv to strike Russian forces while reducing the exposure of its own troops, especially infantry, extend the reach of relatively inexpensive weapons, and compensate for shortages ranging from artillery ammunition to naval power.
Monday’s display brought those strands of the war together in the centre of Kyiv.
Ukraine has not held a conventional military parade since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in early 2022.
In previous years, Khreshchatyk became better known for a very different display of military hardware: burnt-down Russian tanks and armoured vehicles captured or destroyed on the battlefield.

articles.title: Neighbor accuses Sudan of cross-border airstrikes
articles.body:
Neighbor accuses Sudan of cross-border airstrikes
Chad has accused parties in Sudan’s civil war of carrying out airstrikes deep inside its territory, warning that the conflict risks spilling across the border, the Chadian Armed Forces said on Saturday.
According to the statement, aircraft and drones believed to belong to the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) or forces supporting them pursued and bombed a convoy of vehicles on Thursday. The strikes began on Sudanese soil before continuing more than 100 kilometers inside Chad, reaching the Mourdi department in the eastern Ennedi-Est province.
The military said that the extent of the incursion was established following aerial and ground checks conducted on Friday. No Chadian casualties have been reported, but the army condemned what it described as a new violation of the country’s territorial integrity.
Chad warned Sudan’s warring parties against attempting to extend the conflict onto its territory, saying that its defense and security forces remain on the highest level of alert and are prepared to respond to any threat to the country’s security. There has been no response from Sudanese authorities to the Chadian military’s allegations.
Sudan plunged into a civil war three years ago after a struggle for power broke out between the SAF and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army (Sudanese Armed Forces, SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). This occurred after months of tension between their commanders, army generals Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo ‘Hemedti’, respectively, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands and displacing millions.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi–US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. Sudanese officials have named Colombians and Ukrainians among mercenaries backing the RSF against the army. Officials have also accused Ukraine and the United Arab Emirates of involvement and recently claimed the European Union has an “incomplete understanding of the complex situation” in the country.
Khartoum has also accused authorities in neighboring Kenya of backing the RSF and has broken ties with the East African grouping IGAD amid mistrust of regional mediation. In July, TASIS, a political coalition aligned with the paramilitary, announced the formation of a rival government months after its members signed a charter in Nairobi. It named Gen. Dagalo as chairman of a 15-member presidential council, a move rejected by the UN and AU.
The incident follows several previous cases of violence spilling across the Sudan-Chad border. In July, a drone arriving from Sudanese territory struck the eastern Chadian border town of Tine, injuring two children and damaging vehicles and shops, according to local authorities.
In March, a drone strike from Sudan killed at least 17 people in the same town, including mourners attending a funeral. President Mahamat Idriss Deby Itno condemned the attack and ordered the military to retaliate against any future strikes originating from Sudan, whether carried out by the Sudanese army or the RSF.
A month earlier, Chad shut its eastern border with Sudan after five soldiers and three civilians were killed in clashes allegedly involving the SAF and RSF. At least 12 others were wounded in the incident, which also occurred in Tine, officials said.

articles.title: Ukraine requests Patriot missiles from South Korea — newspaper
articles.body:
SEOUL, August 24. /TASS/. Vladimir Zelensky’s senior advisor on strategy, Alexander Kamyshin, visited South Korea in July to request the supply of interceptor missiles for the US-made Patriot air defense systems, but Kiev’s request was turned down, the Chosun Ilbo newspaper reported, citing sources. The request in question was denied on August 10.
"Ukraine, which has been facing shortages of air defense weapons… was reported to have requested South Korea’s support for the latest Patriot interceptor missiles through diplomatic and security channels. South Korean authorities reportedly expressed reluctance, citing reasons such as preparing for contingencies on the Korean Peninsula," the newspaper wrote.
According to Chosun Ilbo, "Alexander Kamyshin, a senior advisor on strategy to Vladimir Zelensky, visited South Korea in early July and met with officials from the Ministry of National Defense and the Defense Acquisition Program Administration. During the meeting, Kamyshin reportedly asked for support for the PAC-3, the latest variant of the US-made interceptor missiles possessed by South Korea."
According to the newspaper, the government "reportedly reviewed internal options, including supporting the domestically produced Cheongung-II surface-to-air missile instead of the Patriot. However, it is widely believed that securing additional production volumes is difficult due to existing export contracts with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE)."
On August 8, Vladimir Zelensky publicly urged South Korea to supply air defense systems. The Chosun Ilbo newspaper called this move "raising the stakes" in the negotiations. On August 10, a high-ranking representative of South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs emphasized that South Korea remained committed to its policy of not supplying lethal weapons to Ukraine.
Seoul has provided financial assistance and supplied non-lethal military items, such as helmets, to Ukraine, but not weapons or ammunition.

articles.title: Israel strikes Gaza as kite threat returns to southern border
articles.body:
The IDF carried out strikes in the Shati refugee camp deep inside the Gaza Strip on Monday, targeting Hamas infrastructure and weapons-storage facilities, amid growing Israeli concern over the reappearance of kites launched from Gaza toward communities near the border.
The targets were located beyond the “yellow line,” which marks the boundary of the area where Israeli forces are currently deployed inside Gaza.
Ahead of the strikes, evacuation warnings were delivered by telephone to several sites in the area, including an elementary school operated by UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, a medical center run by Doctors Without Borders and a compound belonging to the International Rescue Committee.
Palestinians reported that a mosque and a water desalination facility were among the sites struck. There was no immediate information on casualties.
Kites revive memories of prewar threat
At least five kites have been found in recent days in Kibbutz Kfar Aza and Kibbutz Nahal Oz, Israeli communities near the Gaza border. None was carrying incendiary material or explosives.
Authorities believe the kites were launched from the northern Gaza Strip. They carried various messages written in Arabic, including one declaring, “We will never calm down,” in what Israeli officials viewed as an attempt at psychological terror.
Preliminary IDF assessments indicate that children and teenagers launched the kites. Israeli officials say they did so under instructions from Hamas commanders.
The incidents have revived memories among some residents of southern Israel of the years before the current war, when incendiary kites and balloons launched from Gaza initially appeared to pose a limited threat but eventually became a persistent problem, igniting widespread fires in Israeli agricultural fields and nature reserves near the border.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz held a security assessment Sunday to discuss the issue.
“Israel warns Hamas that if the launches toward Israel do not stop immediately, the IDF will step up targeted operations against those responsible for the launches and evacuate populations from areas from which kites, drones and balloons are launched,” a statement issued after the meeting said.
“Israel will not allow the Hamas terrorist organization or any other element in the Gaza Strip to once again threaten our communities and undermine our citizens’ sense of security,” it added.
Israel presses Hamas to disarm
The developments come as the second phase of a plan for Gaza’s reconstruction has yet to formally begin and Israel continues to insist that Hamas disarm.
Southern Command continues to carry out targeted operations inside Gaza, though on a more limited and focused basis. The military says threats to troops along the yellow line are neutralized when detected.
Under current IDF policy, people identified as having participated in the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel can be targeted without requiring additional special authorization, according to Israeli officials.
The military said two Hamas terrorists were killed overnight in the Deir al-Balah area of central Gaza under that policy.

Ukrainian strike drones hit three major Ozon logistics centers across southern Russia, igniting large fires at facilities with a combined warehouse area of more than 314,000 square meters, according to photos and videos published by the OSINT community Exilenova+ on August 24.
The strikes formed part of a much broader Ukrainian operation deep behind Russian lines. Robert “Madyar” Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, said his units successfully engaged 66 Russian targets during the night, including a MiG-29 fighter jet, four radar systems, military facilities and vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet.

“Birds of the Unmanned Systems Forces successfully struck 66 enemy targets in the operational depth of the enemy rear on the night of August 24,” Brovdi said.
Among the most significant targets, according to the commander, was another Russian MiG-29 near Dolotinka in Russia’s Rostov region.
“Among the sensitive targets was another MiG-29 [Dolotinka, Rostov region, Russia] and four radar systems: two Kasta-2E2 units, a Nebo-SV radar [all in Russia’s Rostov region] and an ST-68 radar [Rozdolne, Crimea],” Brovdi said.
He also reported the destruction of a base used by Russia’s SOBR special police forces in occupied Strilkove in Ukraine’s Kherson region, as well as strikes against energy infrastructure across Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory.
Two vessels associated with Russia’s shadow fleet—a tanker and a bulk carrier—were also hit in the Black Sea, Brovdi said. Eleven Russian temporary deployment points were struck across occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
Three Ozon logistics centers were among the most visible targets of the overnight campaign.
The largest was a warehouse complex near Tyube in Russia’s Dagestan region, covering approximately 130,000 square meters. The site serves as a major logistics hub for northern Dagestan and lies roughly 800 to 900 kilometers from Ukraine’s state border.
A major fire erupted following the strike, with local residents reporting that the glow from the blaze could be seen from as far as 10 kilometers away.
Another Ozon logistics center was targeted in Nevinnomyssk, in Russia’s Stavropol region. The facility covers approximately 93,514 square meters.
The third site was an Ozon warehouse near Enem in Adygea, close to the border with Russia’s Krasnodar region. The complex covers about 91,200 square meters. A large fire developed at the facility after the attack.
Ozon is one of Russia’s largest online marketplaces and operates a sprawling logistics network comparable in function to major Western e-commerce platforms.
An investigation earlier found that Russian troops fighting in Ukraine had repeatedly ordered body armor, thermal-imaging equipment, radios, drone batteries, signal boosters, FPV components and payload-release systems through Ozon. Drone-related products were ordered through Ozon particularly frequently.
Ukraine has already put seven of the ten largest logistics centers operated by Russian e-commerce company Wildberries, OZON rival, out of operation.
Wildberries facilities in Domodedovo and at the Koledino industrial park were among the sites affected. The Koledino facility, covering approximately 250,000 square meters, was the company’s largest warehouse by area.

articles.title: Ontario’s premier: Canada should be ready to cut electricity, critical minerals as trade woes worsen
articles.body:
Ontario’s premier: Canada should be ready to cut electricity, critical minerals as trade woes worsen
TORONTO (AP) — Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Monday that Ronald Reagan would be “throwing up” over President Donald Trump’s trade policies and threatened to cut off electricity and critical minerals to the United States as Trump escalated the trade fight.
Ford, speaking in an interview with The Associated Press, said Trump has underestimated Canadians’ willingness to endure economic pain rather than give in to U.S. pressure.
“He underestimates Canada. We’re all in,” Ford said. “Up here, we’re at a fever pitch, everyone’s in for an economic war. They know they’re going to have to sacrifice.”
Trump said Monday that the new 50% tariffs on Canadian automobiles, auto parts and steel would begin next year.
“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trump wrote on social media, criticizing what he called Canada’s “ridiculously high tariffs” on American farmers.
In the AP interview, Ford said Trump had “declared war, economic war against his closest friend and ally” before invoking Reagan, whose opposition to tariffs Ford previously featured in a television advertising campaign aimed at Americans.
Ford noted that Trump keeps a portrait of Reagan near his desk.
“He’d be throwing up on him from the picture if he knew what was going on, spinning around in his grave right now,” Ford said. “He should maybe take that picture off the wall and move it somewhere else. Because right now, Ronald Reagan would be disgusted with President Trump.”
Ford’s comments came after Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from trade negotiations with the Trump administration late Friday, saying Washington demanded too much in exchange for tariff relief. The United States imposed 50% tariffs Saturday on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, while Carney announced dollar-for-dollar retaliation beginning Sept. 8.
Ford threatens critical minerals and electricity
Ford said “everything is on the table” if the dispute worsens, including cutting off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario. He also called for Canada to consider using oil and potash as leverage.
“I’ll cut them off,” Ford said of critical minerals. “You won’t get a grain of sand out of Ontario.”
Critical minerals are increasingly important to U.S. national security and manufacturing. The Pentagon has sought more secure supplies of minerals used in military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics as Washington tries to reduce reliance on China, which dominates the mining or processing of several strategically important minerals.
Ford specifically cited high-grade nickel shipped to the United States and uranium refined in Ontario.
“What would they do without the high-grade nickel that we ship down to the U.S.?” Ford said.
Ford said Canada should consider increasingly severe retaliation if Trump continues targeting Canadian industries, including oil and potash, while Ontario could raise electricity prices or stop sending power south.
“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses,” Ford said. “Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes.”
If Trump continues trying to dismantle Canadian manufacturing, Ford said, “he better have a pack of batteries.”
Ford has used electricity as leverage before. During an earlier phase of the dispute, Ontario imposed a 25% surcharge on electricity exported to Michigan, Minnesota and New York. Trump responded by threatening to double tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum before both sides backed away.
Auto industry becomes a central battleground
Ford accused Trump of seeking not simply a better trade deal but to hollow out Canadian industries and move production south.
Ford said Trump wants to make Canada a vassal state.
“He wants to bleed out every single sector and bring them down to the U.S.,” Ford said.
The auto sector is especially important to Ontario, the center of Canada’s vehicle manufacturing industry. Plants and suppliers in Ontario are tightly integrated with factories in Michigan and other U.S. states, with parts routinely crossing the border multiple times during production.
Automakers including Ford, General Motors and Stellantis operate major assembly plants in Ontario, and the wider supply chain supports tens of thousands of jobs. Trump’s new threat of a 50% tariff on Canadian vehicles and parts puts that sector directly at the center of the escalating dispute.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Monday that “the only reason Canada has auto production in the first place” was because of the 1960s Auto Pact, under which Canada used access to its market to encourage vehicle production north of the border.
“If he thinks the Canadian people are going to roll over and just continue buying American-made vehicles, it’s not going to happen,” Ford said.
Ford says he opposed preliminary deal
Ford also disclosed that he had opposed the preliminary agreement Carney was considering before Canada walked away from the negotiations.
“I wasn’t supporting the deal,” Ford said.
Ford said he was unwilling to restore American liquor to Ontario store shelves as part of an agreement and had been prepared to publicly break with the proposed deal.
“I wasn’t going to put the booze back on the shelves,” Ford said. “I was ready to go out there and call a press conference ... and say I’m not buckling over.”
Ford said he understood Washington had sought language late in the negotiations that would have restricted Canada’s ability to negotiate trade agreements with other countries without U.S. approval. Carney has called that demand unacceptable and a question of Canadian sovereignty.
“Who does he think he is?” Ford said of Trump. “You gotta be kidding.”
Reagan fight returns
Ford’s Reagan comments revived an earlier clash with Trump. Last year, Ontario paid for U.S. television advertisements featuring excerpts from a 1987 Reagan address warning that tariffs can provoke retaliation and trade wars.
Trump accused Ontario of misrepresenting Reagan and abruptly ended trade negotiations with Canada. Ford later agreed to pause the campaign so talks could resume.
“He doesn’t respect anyone,” Ford sad.
Yet despite the increasingly hostile rhetoric, Ford said Canada should remain willing to negotiate.
“I never believe in walking away from the table,” Ford said. “Continue negotiating and see where we go.”
___
Associated Press writer Seung Min Kim contributed from Washington.

MOSCOW, August 24. /TASS/. Russian authorities will now have the power to impose temporary management on critical infrastructure facilities, if their owners fail to implement or restore security measures in a timely manner. This provision is established under a new decree signed by President Vladimir Putin.
According to the decree, the Russian government may assume temporary control over critical infrastructure sites, including the fuel and energy sector, industrial enterprises, communication networks, utilities, transport and logistics infrastructure, and energy facilities such as nuclear power plants - when owners neglect security protocols or delay necessary repairs. The measure also applies to life support systems, potentially hazardous facilities, and other sites vital to the nation's security, economic stability, and public well-being.
The decision to implement these measures stems from the increasing security threats faced by Russia's critical infrastructure amid ongoing operations, and aligns with the laws on Martial Law, Defense, and Security. The decree takes effect immediately upon its official publication.

articles.title: Why Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians in West Bank are pogroms
articles.body:
Why Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians in West Bank are pogroms
Waves of settler attacks, aided by Israel’s military, in the occupied West Bank increasingly fit the definition of a pogrom.
Attacks on Palestinian communities by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, which are often supported by Israeli forces, have gathered pace over the past month since settlers from the Havat Gilad settlement attacked Palestinian homes on the eastern edge of Tal, southwest of Nablus.
On Sunday and Monday, the Israeli military raided multiple towns, villages and refugee camps across the occupied territory, and reports of arrests, home searches and settler attacks have continued to mount.
A 15-day siege on three families comprising 15 people, including two children, in the village of Qusra, which is ongoing, drew a rare public condemnation this month from the United States ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, a staunch supporter of Israel and its West Bank settlements.
Israel is also pushing ahead with plans for the so-called E1 settlement expansion close to Jerusalem, which human rights organisations warn would essentially sever the West Bank in two, further hampering the freedom of movement of Palestinians on either side of it and endangering the possibility of a Palestinian state.
The West Bank attacks increasingly fit the definition of a pogrom, experts said. United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories Francesca Albanese described these Israeli attacks against Palestinians as “pogroms against defenceless civilians”.
So why are experts calling settler attacks pogroms, and do they fit the formal definition of one?
What’s happening in the West Bank?
Settlers, frequently supported by the Israeli military, have been attacking Palestinian homes, businesses, and agricultural fields across the occupied West Bank. Such attacks have been commonplace for decades as settlements have expanded across the territory, but they gathered pace after October 7, 2023 when Israel launched it genocidal war on Gaza, and have become particularly violent and frequent over the past month.
Israeli settlements across the West Bank are illegal under international law.
According to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, however, Israeli settlers now number roughly 780,000 across the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, living among 192 settlements and 400 outposts, rising to 71 percent of Area C, which is under full Israeli civil and military control, and 91 percent of the Jordan Valley.
Settlers often set up outposts without formal approval around Palestinian villages from which they launch a campaign of harassment, including killing livestock, cutting supply lines and damaging property, in order to drive local residents out. Once they establish a more formal settlement, they often receive retrospective approval from the Israeli government for the settlement.
In some places more recently, illegal settlers have laid siege to individual family homes – such as in the Ras al-Ein area of Qusra – cutting off water and other supplies and damaging orchards or harming livestock.
This has set a new pattern: settlers establish a tent adjacent to individual homes; Palestinians’ homes are besieged, with essentials cut off; and Israeli soldiers arrive not to remove the settlers, but rather to remove the family – through arrest or ostensibly for their “protection”.
In Qusra, the three besieged families were forced together into one of the family houses. Meanwhile, Israeli forces have occupied one of the other homes for use as a military post and thrown furniture and belongings from its windows, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
The UN humanitarian affairs office recorded more than 1,330 settler-related attacks on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank between January and late July this year, averaging six a day and marking the fastest pace since the agency began systematic tracking two decades ago.
Separately, a UN-appointed commission of inquiry has found that the Israeli authorities have repeatedly failed to prevent foreseeable settler attacks and, in some cases, have directly enabled them through army protection and the provision of weapons and funding.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has found that settler attacks, demolitions and evictions forcibly displaced more Palestinians in the first four months of this year than in the whole of 2025.
OCHA reported that 107 communities, comprising 5,900 Palestinians, had been completely or partially displaced as a result of settler violence since January 2023. It also found that the Israeli military have expelled another 32,000 Palestinians from their homes in the occupied West Bank since January 2025, essentially emptying the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams camps.
What is the definition of a pogrom?
Major US and UK dictionaries vary to some degree on the definition of a “pogrom”.
The British Collins Dictionary identifies a pogrom as “organised, official violence against a group of people for racial or religious reasons”, with a notable inclusion of official, or state-backed violence.
Oxford Advanced Learner’s Dictionary calls it “the organised killing of large numbers of people, because of their race or religion”, without mention of state-sanctioned violence.
Merriam-Webster says it is “an organised massacre of helpless people” – “specifically: such as a massacre of Jews”.
Cambridge Dictionary says it is “an act of organised cruel behaviour or killing that is done to a large group of people because of their race or religion”.
The word is understood to have been introduced via Yiddish and was at first used to describe the wave of violent, organised mob attacks on Jewish communities in the Russian Empire following the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in 1881.
It is important to note that unlike legal terms including “crimes against humanity” or “genocide,” “pogrom” has no established legal definition under international law.
Can attacks in the West Bank be referred to as pogroms?
Besides Francesca Albanese, the UN Special Rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, who has described Israeli attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank as “pogroms against defenceless civilians”, Israeli officials themselves have described such attacks as “pogroms”.
On February 26, 2023, hundreds of Israeli settlers attacked Huwara and surrounding Palestinian communities after two Israeli settlers were killed. A Palestinian was killed, hundreds were injured, and homes, businesses and cars were burned.
The Israeli military’s then-commander in the occupied West Bank, Yehuda Fuchs, called the settlers’ attack a “pogrom”, and it was also recorded as such by the US State Department.
Israeli-Palestinian human rights group B’Tselem has also previously described Israeli actions in the occupied West Bank as “pogroms”, especially after the February 2023 attacks. Later, it followed up with a report titled, “The pogroms are working – the transfer is already happening”, which argued that settler attacks were contributing to the displacement of Palestinian communities.
“Settler violence is not a new phenomenon. But over the past three years, it has become more violent, more systematic and, most importantly, part of a state mechanism intended to ethnically cleanse large parts of the West Bank,” said Yair Dvir, the spokesperson for B’Tselem.
“The government funds and arms the settlers, while the Israeli military stands by and, in many cases, actively participates in the attacks,” he told Al Jazeera. “So far, these militias have expelled 64 Palestinian communities and taken control of around one million dunams of land.”
Dvir also told Al Jazeera that the Israeli settlers are “now carrying out organised attacks on established Palestinian villages and towns in order to drive out their residents”.
“These are armed militias operating as an unofficial arm of the state, with a shared goal: to ethnically cleanse as much of the West Bank as possible,” he added.
The Lemkin Institute for Genocide Prevention, which is named after Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin, who is credited with coining the term genocide after the Holocaust, referred to settler attacks on Al-Mughayyir, a Palestinian village in Ramallah, as “pogroms”, reporting that hundreds of armed settlers attacked residents and burned buildings and cars while soldiers stood by earlier this year. In 2025, the Israeli military uprooted thousands of Palestinian olive trees at Al-Mughayyir.
Raheel Dhattiwala, an Indian scholar who focuses on collective violence, told Al Jazeera: “West Bank attacks fit the characteristics of a pogrom – systematic targeting of one civilian group by another with state approval. A few senior Israeli army officers have called it ‘pogroms’ in the past too, for example after attacks in Huwara.
“One might want to debate the use of the term, ‘pogrom’, but it is accurate to call settler violence systematic attacks of occupiers, with government approval, on groups of occupied people.”

articles.title: Ex-Pussy Riot Member Says She Helped the FSB Spy on Kremlin Critics
articles.body:
Former Pussy Riot member Rita Flores has revealed that she was coerced into working as an informant for Russia’s FSB security service, saying that she gathered information on anti-war activists and was involved in a failed assassination plot against an exiled Kremlin critic.
Flores said FSB officers coerced her into signing a cooperation agreement following a February 2023 raid on her Moscow apartment, threatening her with criminal prosecution over social media posts about alleged Russian war crimes in Ukraine alongside death threats against her relatives.
“They began recruiting me with all kinds of threats and abuse [including] threats to murder my family and that I’d never be able to prove who killed my mother,” she told the exiled news outlet Port in a video interview.
Operating under the codename “Harley,” Flores said she was assigned to build detailed profiles on Russian artists and political dissidents. Between early 2024 and June, she received monthly payments of 50,000 rubles ($600) from her security service handlers after an initial disbursement of 30,000 rubles ($360).
Flores detailed how she deliberately sabotaged her FSB assignments for over two years, faking personal feuds with targets like artists Philippenzo and Pavel Krisevich to delay their arrest by law enforcement authorities.
In mid-2025, Flores said she was ordered to lure her ex-boyfriend and former Pussy Riot member Pyotr Verzilov into a cafe in Serbia where undercover FSB agents planned to kidnap and kill him. The activist said she was offered 3 million rubles ($36,000) for her role in that assassination plot.
“That was the point of no return. Before, I thought I just needed to wait to get my passport back and flee. But then I realized how far they were willing to go,” Flores said in the interview with Port.
Refusing to help carry out the assassination plot against Verzilov, Flores stalled her handlers and sought help from human rights lawyer Dmitry Zakhvatov. Exiled businessman Leonid Nevzlin subsequently helped her flee Russia earlier this month.
The Moscow Times could not independently verify any of the claims made by Flores.

articles.title: Ukraine returns 10 servicemen its own records had marked missing in action
articles.body:
Ukraine brought a small group of servicemen home from captivity on 24 August, its Independence Day, and every one of them had been carried as missing in action, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced. The men crossed back through Belarus as a separate stage of the exchange now under way. Ukraine's prisoner-of-war agency later set out who they were.
Amid Russia's all-out war in Ukraine, prisoner swaps remain one of the few Ukrainian-Russian mechanisms still producing results while every negotiating track on territory and ceasefires stays deadlocked, which leaves each completed stage as the practical measure of what still passes between two governments that agree on nothing else.
Ten men Ukraine had listed as missing, not captured
President Zelenskyy said Ukraine was bringing back 10 of its soldiers through Belarus. They serve in the Armed Forces and the National Guard, and they defended the country in the Donetsk sector in the east. He called it a special stage of the exchange.
The Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, the state body that runs Ukraine's exchanges, specified the details in the afternoon. The freed men hold the ranks of sergeant, soldier, and sailor. All 10 had been logged as missing rather than captured.
Two had been listed as missing since 2024, the other eight since 2025. The agency said the handover came out of talks run by its own exchange working group. It described the return as the second stage of the current exchange.
The first stage ran on 19 August and brought back 103 servicemen.
Locating Ukrainian captives inside Russia or the occupied territories is often difficult, as is verifying their identities, because Russia withholds data on captured soldiers and civilian hostages. Former detainees describe beatings, electric shocks, mock executions, and refusals of medical care, and civilians held without trial report the same treatment as the soldiers.
Roughly 7,000 Ukrainian service members were in Russian captivity as of May 2026, with civilian detainees estimated at 10,000 to 20,000. Ukraine had returned 9,606 military personnel and civilians through exchanges by late June.

articles.title: Iran says not to let war end based on "aggressive" parties' conditions
articles.body:
TEHRAN, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that his country will not let the war end based on conditions set by the "aggressive" parties.
"We have definitely not been the party to start the war, but we will not let the war's end be based on the aggressive parties' conditions," Baghaei told a weekly press conference in Tehran.
He said that Iran remained determined to defend its territory and would not "compromise with the aggressive parties" or surrender to their "excessive demands."
Baghaei dismissed U.S. claims that the Strait of Hormuz was open and that millions of barrels of oil were passing through it each day, describing them as part of "psychological and media warfare."
He also slammed Washington's newly announced anti-Iran economic operation, saying Tehran would use all its "multilateral capacities" to counter U.S. sanctions, which he described as a blow to free trade and national sovereignty.
The spokesman also warned that countries assisting U.S. anti-Iran operations could face consequences, and called the U.S. naval blockade an "act of aggression."
Asked about Western media reports that Iran could target U.S. bases in Europe if war resumed, Baghaei said Iran reserved the right to target the origin and source of any "act of aggression" if another country allowed its bases, facilities and equipment to be used for such actions.
Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities on Feb. 28, killing then-Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, military commanders and civilians. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz, barring passage of vessels belonging to or affiliated with Israel and the United States.
A ceasefire was achieved between the warring parties on April 8. On June 18, Iran and the United States signed a memorandum of understanding on ending the war on all fronts, including Lebanon.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Wednesday announced "the most crushing economic operation ever taken" against any country providing a lifeline to Iran, calling the move "an ECONOMIC D-DAY." ■

articles.title: Zelenskyy sums up Coalition of the Willing meeting in Kyiv: aid packages and air defence listed as priorities
articles.body:
Zelenskyy sums up Coalition of the Willing meeting in Kyiv: aid packages and air defence listed as priorities
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Kyiv will receive military and energy aid packages following a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Kyiv on 24 August.
Source: Zelenskyy speaking after the meeting, as reported by European Pravda
Quote: "Support for Ukraine will continue. Air defence is a priority."
Details: Zelenskyy said Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi has briefed Ukraine's partners on the country's financial needs.
The Ukrainian leader also said that French President Emmanuel Macron has proposed that efforts to counter Russia's shadow fleet be stepped up and that a separate meeting be held on the issue.
"Europe must have a seat at the negotiating table. In any case, I'll be honest: many of the leaders who spoke today are genuinely sceptical about whether Putin is willing to engage in any negotiations at this point," Zelenskyy added.
Background:
- UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said London has approved the decision to share Storm Shadow production technology with Ukraine.
- Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has announced a new aid package for Ukraine.

articles.title: BeiDou support tops 98 pct of China's H1 phone shipments as commercial adoption broadens
articles.body:
BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- More than 98 percent of the 133 million mobile phones shipped in China's domestic market in the first half (H1) of 2026 supported the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS), as this technology expands across consumer devices, transport and other industries, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) said on Monday.
Over 14 million shared two-wheelers had adopted BeiDou independent positioning by the end of June, accounting for more than 90 percent of the country's total fleet.
These figures highlight the growing rollout of BeiDou, China's global satellite navigation system, across consumer and industrial applications.
At a media roundtable on large-scale BeiDou applications, Shi Huikang, deputy director of the MIIT's department of electronic information, said China has stepped up pilot programs, product promotion, standards development and ecosystem building in recent years to accelerate adoption.
China's domestic supply base has also continued to expand. By the end of 2025, cumulative shipments of domestically produced BeiDou-compatible chips and modules had approached 2.6 billion units, while the installed base of terminal products with BeiDou functions had exceeded 2.2 billion units, according to the ministry.
Authorities have also supported the development and commercialization of high-precision, interference-resistant and low-power products, helping improve performance and lower costs.
Deployment has also expanded across 39 pilot cities for large-scale BeiDou applications, which had introduced more than 12 million terminals using BeiDou independent positioning by the end of June.
In a number of cities, designated sectors including shared two-wheelers, taxis, government vehicles, agricultural machinery and police equipment have achieved 100-percent BeiDou adoption, the ministry said.
BeiDou's footprint is also expanding across major industries. China now has nearly 40 million BeiDou terminal devices in key sectors, where overall application penetration stands at about 90 percent. More than 160 million wearable devices support BeiDou positioning, while over 100 million passenger vehicles have been equipped with BeiDou-based positioning devices.
Industry data released in May revealed the scale of the broader market. China's satellite navigation industry generated 629 billion yuan (roughly 92.7 billion U.S. dollars) in output in 2025, up 9.24 percent year on year, according to a white paper released by the Global Navigation Satellite System and Location-Based Services Association of China.
The white paper also said BeiDou services and related products have been exported to more than 140 countries and regions worldwide. It said the sector is upgrading toward a broader BeiDou spatiotemporal industry integrating satellite navigation with mobile communications, indoor positioning and artificial intelligence.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the MIIT said it will work with other authorities to support breakthroughs in key technologies and their industrial application, while continuing pilot programs for large-scale BeiDou deployment.
The ministry also plans to foster a broader spatiotemporal information industry by promoting coordinated development across satellite positioning, navigation and timing, remote sensing, geographic information systems, communications and satellite internet. ■

articles.title: Israel subjecting Russian historian to brutal interrogation – lawyer
articles.body:
Israel subjecting Russian historian to brutal interrogation – lawyer
Russian-Israeli historian Artyom Kirpichenok has been subjected to brutal treatment while in Shin Bet custody, including interrogations lasting up to 24 hours, sleep deprivation, prolonged handcuffing, and threats, according to his lawyer.
Kirpichenok, 51, disappeared on August 2 shortly after arriving at Ben Gurion Airport from Yerevan. His whereabouts remained unknown for nearly three weeks before his supporters revealed that he was being held at a detention facility in Petah Tikva.
His lawyer, Inna Lebedinskaya-Katz, was finally allowed to meet with him for around an hour on Sunday after repeatedly seeking access, according to Nika Dubrovsky, a Russian-born artist and writer campaigning for his release.
Citing Lebedinskaya-Katz, Dubrovsky said Kirpichenok has faced interrogation sessions lasting 18 to 24 hours while deprived of sleep. He is allegedly being kept handcuffed and hunched over on an iron stool fixed to the floor, with three or four interrogators standing behind him “shouting, threatening, and applying constant pressure.” He has also allegedly been threatened with life imprisonment.
Kirpichenok is in “tolerable physical condition” and has no immediate health complaints, but is “exhausted, tormented and deeply depressed,” Dubrovsky wrote on X on Monday.
”He understands that his friends have not abandoned him. He is holding on and sends his greetings to everyone,” she wrote. Kirpichenok also asked that no one come to Israel.
The allegations have not been independently verified. However, international human rights groups previously documented sleep deprivation and painful restraint during Shin Bet interrogations. Israel’s Supreme Court has ruled against deliberately using prolonged sleep deprivation to break suspects.
Kirpichenok is being held underground with the lights on around the clock and denied books and writing materials, Dubrovsky cited his lawyer as saying. A gag order remains in force, and the defense has yet to receive the case files or details of the accusations.
Kirpichenok, a dual Russian-Israeli citizen and Middle East expert, is known for criticizing Israel’s policies toward Iran and Palestine. Moscow sought information from the Israeli authorities following his disappearance and said it is closely monitoring the case.
Kirpichenok recently worked with media outlets and civic organizations in Türkiye and Iran and frequently traveled to Iran. Israeli citizens are generally prohibited from traveling to countries they are at war with. Dubrovsky, however, said the trips now appear to be of little interest to investigators.
Born in Russia, Kirpichenok moved to Israel in the 1990s, studied at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and served in the Israel Defense Forces before returning to Russia. He later became a vocal critic of the Israeli government and its military campaign in Gaza, describing Israel as a Western “colonial project” in his recent book ‘Israel: The Road to Catastrophe’.
The Israeli authorities have yet to publicly disclose any charges against him.

articles.title: ‘We don’t need Canada’: Trump threatens to double auto tariffs after trade talks collapse
articles.body:
‘We don’t need Canada’: Trump threatens to double auto tariffs after trade talks collapse
US tariffs on all Canadian cars and trucks, automotive parts and steel will be increased to 50% starting January 1, 2027, President Donald Trump said in a social post on Monday. Doubling down on his threats, Trump said the US does not “need” Canada after trade talks between the two countries collapsed over the weekend.
